Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The current paradigm of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has generated a massive ecosystem of task-specific Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters. However, utilizing these specialized modules simultaneously presents a significant integration challenge. Existing frameworks largely rely on explicit, manual "task intention" signals—requiring a user or system to pre-select which adapter to load for a specific prompt. This static approach fails during "composite tasks," where a model must sequentially address multiple distinct sub-problems (e.g., logical reasoning followed by translation) within a single inference pass. There is currently no efficient mechanism for a Large Language Model (LLM) to autonomously sense the context and dynamically switch between multiple embedded adapters token-by-token.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can convert a library of independent, pre-trained LoRA adapters into a unified, autonomous system by structuring them as "experts" within a full-mode Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. By training a lightweight gating mechanism to route inputs to the appropriate fixed adapters, the model should be able to perform on-demand skill switching without human intervention. We further posit that the computational bottleneck of accessing these disjoint experts can be overcome by parallelizing the adapter computations via batched matrix operations, rather than sequential execution.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to develop a framework that integrates multiple existing LoRA adapters into a frozen base LLM.

*   **MoE-Style Integration:** We will treat the low-rank matrices from various pre-trained adapters as the "experts" in an MoE layer. This module will be injected into the linear layers of the base Transformer (both Attention and MLP blocks).
*   **Learnable Gating Network:** We will introduce a trainable router (gate) alongside the frozen experts. This gate will take the input hidden state and output a probability distribution over the available adapters.
*   **Dynamic Routing & Fusion:** For each token, the gate will select the top-$k$ most relevant adapters. The final output of the layer will be the base model's output plus the weighted sum of the projections from the selected low-rank matrices.
*   **Training Strategy:** We will freeze the parameters of the base LLM and the reused LoRA adapters. We will optimize *only* the parameters of the gating network. The loss function will be a joint objective combining standard autoregressive language modeling loss with a classification loss to encourage precise expert selection.
*   **Forward Acceleration:** To address the latency issues inherent in naive MoE implementations (which typically use slow iterative loops to process different experts), we will design a parallelized forward pass. We aim to implement a strategy utilizing batched matrix multiplications to compute expert outputs simultaneously. To handle the potential memory overhead of this parallelization, we will explore custom GPU kernel operators that optimize the loading of adapter matrices from high-bandwidth memory.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Autonomous Multi-Adapter Orchestration:** A methodology enabling LLMs to utilize dozens of off-the-shelf adapters simultaneously without manual task specification.
*   **Composite Task Capability:** Theoretical validation that fine-grained, token-level adapter switching enables models to solve complex problems requiring sequential domain shifts.
*   **Efficient MoE Inference:** A novel algorithmic approach to accelerating MoE forward passes, specifically targeting the efficiency bottlenecks of serving multiple LoRA modules.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the "MeteoRA" (Multiple-tasks embedded LoRA) framework against various baselines.

*   **Base Models:**
    *   LlaMA2-13B
    *   LlaMA3-8B
    *   Both models were pretrained and utilized without instruction tuning for the base.

*   **Hardware & Compute:**
    *   Training/Inference Server: GPU server with five H800 80G GPUs.
    *   Training Time: Gating networks for 28 tasks took <10 hours to reach convergence on 4 H800s.
    *   Inference Efficiency Tests: Batch size × 10 samples truncated from test sets.

*   **Datasets & Tasks:**
    *   **Total Tasks:** 28 tasks selected from established benchmarks.
    *   **Sources:**
        *   BigBench (22 tasks)
        *   News-Commentary (3 tasks: German, Spanish, Italian to English translation)
        *   GSM8K (Mathematics)
        *   CNN/DailyMail (Summarization)
        *   Alpaca (Instruction following)
    *   **Data Splits:**
        *   *LoRA Training:* Original training sets of respective tasks.
        *   *Gating Network Training (Balanced):* 1,000 samples randomly sampled per task (900 train / 100 validation).
        *   *Limited Data Scenarios:* We also tested scenarios with only 100 and 5 samples per task.
        *   *Evaluation:* Original test sets for each task.
    *   **Composite Datasets:** Constructed for sequential task evaluation.
        *   *Composite-3:* 3 tasks concatenated, 200 samples. Temperature set to 15.
        *   *Composite-5:* 5 tasks concatenated, 200 samples. Temperature set to 20.
        *   *Composite-10:* 10 tasks concatenated, 200 samples. Temperature set to 30.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Zero-shot setting** used for all individual tasks.
    *   **Metric Assignment:**
        *   Accuracy: Multiple-choice tasks, GSM8K, extractive tasks.
        *   Generation Metrics (BLEU, ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L): Translation, Summarization, Alpaca, etc.
    *   **Composite Metrics:** Average number of attempts, Average number correct (multiple choice), Average BLEU/ROUGE (generation components).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **LoRA Configuration:** Rank $r=8$, $\alpha=16$.
    *   **Optimization:** Learning rate $5e-5$. Batch size 4 (for fine-tuning).
    *   **Gating Strategies:** Top-1 (standard selection) and Top-2 (mixing).
    *   **Forward Acceleration:** Implemented `bmm-torch` (batched matrix multiplication in PyTorch) and `bmm-triton` (custom Triton kernel) to optimize MoE forward passes.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **PEFT (Reference):** Huggingface PEFT loading all 28 adapters with *explicit* activation (oracle task ID provided).
    *   **LoRA-F:** Single LoRA adapter trained on a mixed dataset of all 28 tasks.
    *   **LoRA-B:** Single LoRA adapter trained on the balanced dataset (same data used for Gate training).
    *   **Merge Methods:** Avg Merge (Averaging weights), TIES, DARE, Arrow, LoRAHub.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Performance Maintenance:** MeteoRA utilizing the top-1 strategy achieved performance very close to the reference model (PEFT with explicit oracle instructions), demonstrating that performance can be maintained without explicit LoRA activation/deactivation instructions.
*   **LoRA Mixing (Top-2 Strategy):** MeteoRA with the top-2 strategy occasionally outperformed the reference PEFT model, suggesting that mixing LoRA adapters from different tasks can be beneficial.
*   **Low-Resource Efficiency:** MeteoRA models trained with limited data (100 or 5 samples) still outperformed baseline models on most metrics, indicating the gating network learns effectively with few-shot examples.
*   **Composite Task Performance:** MeteoRA consistently outperformed LoRA-B in composite tasks (composite-5 and composite-10) across almost all metrics. While MeteoRA attempted slightly fewer questions in composite-3 tasks, it correctly answered a higher number of multiple-choice questions.
*   **Dynamic LoRA Switching:** Visual analysis of token-level LoRA selection in composite tasks confirmed that the Gating network assigns greater weight to the relevant LoRA adapters for the majority of tokens and correctly switches adapters at the junctions of adjacent tasks (e.g., switching from logical deduction to question selection).
*   **Runtime Efficiency:** The `bmm-torch` forward pass design achieved approximately a 4x speedup compared to the `loop-original` implementation. It was approximately 2.5x slower than the theoretical upper-bound (`single-lora`).
*   **Memory Efficiency:** The `bmm-triton` implementation achieved approximately 80% of the performance of `bmm-torch` while maintaining a low memory footprint similar to `loop-original`, mitigating out-of-memory risks associated with `bmm-torch` on large batch/sequence tasks.
*   **Cross-Lingual Knowledge Fusion:** In a specific experiment involving mathematics problems translated into a foreign language (Italian), MeteoRA successfully fused GSM8K (English math) and translation LoRAs but did not outperform the base LLM equipped only with the GSM8K LoRA.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The pretrain-fine-tune paradigm has enabled Large Language Models (LLMs) to adapt to downstream tasks efficiently, particularly via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). While this produces high-quality, task-specific adapters, current deployment frameworks (such as Huggingface PEFT or S-LoRA) suffer from a critical rigidity: they require explicit, manual task intention selection. Users must specify which adapter to load before inference. This prevents the model from autonomously sensing the task context or switching capabilities dynamically during a single inference pass (e.g., handling composite tasks that require multiple distinct skills sequentially). Furthermore, existing MoE-style fusion attempts are often limited to specific modules (FFN only) or lack the computational efficiency required for scaling to large numbers of off-the-shelf adapters.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **MeteoRA (Multiple-tasks embedded LoRA)**, a framework that converts a library of pre-trained, static LoRA adapters into a dynamic Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) system. By embedding a trainable Gating network into every linear layer of the base LLM, we hypothesize that the model can learn to autonomously route input tokens to the most relevant LoRA adapter(s) without explicit user instruction.

We further hypothesize that the inference latency inherent in "loop-based" MoE implementations can be mitigated through custom GPU kernel operations. By implementing specific `bmm-torch` (batched matrix multiplication) and `bmm-triton` (fused kernel) strategies, we expect to achieve near-native inference speeds while maintaining the memory footprint of standard loading methods.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. MeteoRA Architecture
We will integrate $n$ existing, pre-trained LoRA adapters $\{ L_1, L_2, \dots, L_n \}$ into a base LLM $\mathcal{M}$. Each adapter $L_i$ consists of low-rank matrices $\{ A_i, B_i \}$. We will not fine-tune these adapters; they are treated as frozen experts.

Instead, we will inject a trainable **Gating network** $\dot{\boldsymbol{G}}: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^n$ into every basic linear layer of the Transformer architecture. This includes the attention modules ($W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o$) and the MLP modules ($W_{up}, W_{gating}, W_{down}$).

For an input token hidden state $\pmb{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the Gating network will calculate logits $G(\pmb{x})$ to select the top-$k$ indices, denoted as $I(\pmb{x}) := \{i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k\}$. The forward pass for the MeteoRA-enhanced layer is defined as:

$$ o = x W_{\mathrm{base}} + \sum_{i \in I(x)} w_i \cdot \left( \left( x \times A_i \right) \times B_i \right) $$

Here, $w_i$ represents the normalized weight of the selected LoRA adapter $L_i$, calculated via softmax over the selected top-$k$ experts:

$$ w_i = \text{softmax}(G_i(\pmb{x})) = \frac{\exp(G_i(\pmb{x}))}{\sum_{j \in I(\pmb{x})} \exp(G_j(\pmb{x}))} $$

This architecture allows different MeteoRA modules across different layers to make independent routing decisions, enabling dynamic adapter switching within a single forward pass.

### 2. Learning Algorithm and Optimization
We will freeze the parameters of the base model $\mathcal{M}$ and all LoRA matrices $\{ A_i, B_i \}$. Only the parameters of the Gating networks will be trainable. We will define a joint optimization objective that combines the autoregressive language modeling loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lm}}$ with a Gating network classification loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gate}}$.

The total loss function $\mathcal{L}$ is formulated as:

$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lm}} + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gate}} = \mathop{\arg\max}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^{L} (\log \mathrm{P}(x_i \mid x_{i-1}; \theta) + \beta \sum_{j=1}^{B} \sum_{k=1}^{m} l_{k,j}(h)) $$

Where:
*   $\beta$ is a hyper-parameter balancing the losses.
*   $L$ is the sequence length.
*   $B$ is the number of decoder blocks.
*   $m$ is the number of MeteoRA modules per block.
*   $l_{k,j}(h)$ is the cross-entropy loss for LoRA classification (prediction of the correct expert) given hidden input $h$.

### 3. Forward Acceleration Strategies
To overcome the efficiency bottleneck of naive MoE implementations (which iterate through experts in a loop), we will develop two acceleration strategies:

**A. bmm-torch (Batched Matrix Multiplication)**
We will parallelize the computation for all $b \times s \times k$ tokens and $n$ adapters simultaneously using batched operations:

$$ \Delta o_{1 \dots bs} = \sum_{k} [w_1, \dots, w_{bsk}] \odot \left( \left( [x_1, \dots, x_{bsk}] \times [A_{i_1}, \dots, A_{i_{bsk}}] \right) \times [B_{i_1}, \dots, B_{i_{bsk}}] \right) $$

This method trades memory for speed by allocating space for batched matrices.

**B. bmm-triton (Custom Fused Kernel)**
To resolve the memory overhead of `bmm-torch`, we will implement a custom GPU kernel using **Triton**. This kernel will fuse the two matrix multiplications and dynamically index the correct pair $(A_i, B_i)$ from High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to SRAM, avoiding explicit allocation of full batched matrices.

To address Triton's dimension constraint (dimensions must be $\ge 16$) given that LoRA rank $r$ is often small (e.g., $r=8$), we will employ a **blocking strategy**. We will split the vector $\pmb{x}$ along the hidden size dimension into blocks of size $m$ (where $m \ge 16$).
The kernel logic will perform:
1.  Blockized loading of $X$ and $A'$.
2.  Computation of $oA' = X \times A'$.
3.  Masking and column summation: $oA'' = ((oA' \odot M_1) \times M_2)$, where $M_1, M_2$ are mask matrices to handle dimension mismatches.
4.  Final multiplication with $B$: $oB' = oA'' \times B$.

This approach ensures the system is both time-efficient (via parallelization) and memory-efficient (via fused operations).

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Scalable Autonomous Integration:** We expect to demonstrate a framework where dozens of off-the-shelf LoRA adapters can be embedded into a single LLM, enabling the model to autonomously select and switch between tasks (e.g., translation to math) within a single generation without user intervention.
2.  **Full-Mode MoE Architecture:** By converting all linear layers (Attention and MLP) into MoE modules, we anticipate superior performance on composite tasks compared to single-task adapters or simple merging techniques.
3.  **High-Performance Inference:** The proposed `bmm-triton` kernel is expected to achieve inference speeds roughly $4\times$ faster than naive loop-based MoE implementations, making multi-adapter deployment practically viable.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
